70.0.s.en: (5) Praise to God who saves His children

70.0.0.en: 1- Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O Lord.

70.0.1.en: David was in severe suffering in his trial, so he asked God for deliverance, indeed for haste in helping him. This shows his faith in God, his feeling of his great need of Him, and his hard suffering which he could not bear; therefore he asked God for swift help.

70.1.0.en: 2- Let them be ashamed and confounded that seek after my soul: let them be turned backward, and put to confusion, that desire my hurt.

70.1.1.en: David believed that God would save him from the hands of his enemies, and consequently shame would cover them. Likewise, those who desire David's harm and destruction will fear and turn backward before the power of God who rescues David.

70.2.0.en: 3- Let them be turned back for a reward of their shame that say, Aha, aha.

70.2.1.en: When those who want to destroy David are put to shame, and those who desire his harm draw back, then all who gloated over David will also be put to shame and draw back, those who mocked him when he was suffering in his trial and raised their voices against him in derision, saying, "Aha, aha."

70.3.0.en: 4- Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: and let such as love thy salvation say continually, Let the Lord be magnified.

70.3.1.en: On the other hand, David calls all the righteous who cling to God to rejoice and be glad in the salvation of God which they have received, and then to glorify God and magnify Him. Thus the children of God spend their days, rejoicing in salvation and glorifying the name of the holy God.

70.4.0.en: 5- But I am poor and needy: make haste unto me, O God: thou art my help and my deliverer; O Lord, make no tarrying. At the end of the Psalm David declares his humility and his need before God, so he asks for God's help and His constant salvation for him; because the enemy, Satan, never rests, but repeats his attacks and stirs up the wicked against the one who walks in God's commandments, so David needs God's constant protection.

70.4.1.en: Be sure that your God is waiting for your prayers in order to answer you; for He loves you and died for you on the Cross. So do not be slack in asking for His help, and when afflictions increase upon you, cry out to Him, confident that He will keep you and deliver you, and you will glorify Him.

70.4.3.en: "In thee, O Lord, do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion" (v. 1). Introduction:

70.4.4.en: 1- Its writer: a- This Psalm is one of the orphan Psalms, that is, those whose writer is not named in the title; but many of the Fathers attribute this Psalm to David.

70.4.5.en: b- Some see that its writer is the prophet Jeremiah, because its style is similar to Jeremiah's style, and also the events that Jeremiah went through (v. 20).

70.4.7.en: If its writer is David, then it was at the end of his life, when Absalom drove him out, or any other afflictions that met him in his old age.

70.4.9.en: In the Septuagint, the title of the Psalm reads, "Of David. A Psalm sung by the sons of Jonadab." This Jonadab is the son of Rechab, that is, the descendants of the Rechabites who held fast to the teachings of their father not to drink wine, nor build houses, nor plant vineyards (Jer 35:5-10); that is, they lived relying on God.

70.4.10.en: 4- The title of this Psalm in the Septuagint also contains "and of those who were led into captivity", which means that the Psalm prophesies about the period of the captivity and the sufferings that the people of God endured as they went into captivity (v. 20).

70.4.11.en: 5- This Psalm resembles Psalm 31 in its beginning, and resembles Psalm 35 in its ending. Thus we find (vv. 1-3) resembling (Ps 31:1-3), and also the verses (vv. 23, 24) resembling (Ps 35:26-28).

70.4.12.en: 6- This Psalm is full of feelings of faith in the power of God who supports His children, and it calls whoever says it to thanksgiving and praise. It is therefore suitable for every person passing through affliction, so that his faith and his love for God may be strengthened.

70.4.13.en: 7- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.

71.0.s.en: (1) God my fortress and my rock

71.0.0.en: 1- In thee, O Lord, do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion.

71.0.1.en: The writer of the Psalm speaks from an experience of faith: he asked for God's protection, found great help, and consequently was lifted up above his enemies. He was not put to shame, that is, God did not neglect him; on the contrary, his enemies were put to shame. This confirms the strength of his faith by which he lives all his life. This verse also shows the fatherhood of God and His care, who does not forsake His children forever; He keeps them in this life and gives them joy in the life to come.

71.1.0.en: 2- Deliver me in thy righteousness, and cause me to escape: incline thine ear unto me, and save me.

71.1.1.en: 1- Having become sure of the power of God which supports him, David asked Him to rescue him from the affliction he was passing through. David asked God to rescue him by His justice, and this shows David's reliance on the justice of God, and his innocence of the accusations that his enemies direct at him.

71.1.2.en: 2- David's asking God to incline His ear to him shows two things:

71.1.3.en: a- David's declaration of his weakness, since his voice is feeble.

71.1.4.en: b- David's confidence in God's tenderness and humility, that He inclines His ear and condescends and draws near to him. This was fulfilled in the Incarnation of Christ in the fullness of time, when He came down to us from heaven to redeem us and give us life.

71.2.0.en: 3- Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort: thou hast given commandment to save me; for thou art my rock and my fortress.

71.2.1.en: 1- David asks God to be a fortress for him, that is, a very strong place which he enters and takes refuge in, so that no one can harm him. This shows David's faith in the power of God, and at the same time his great need of Him.

71.2.2.en: 2- What is wonderful is David's faith after this petition, for he trusted that God had heard him and would answer him, save him and protect him. So he said in the past tense, "Thou hast given commandment to save me", that is, he believes that God has answered and commanded, and only the carrying out of His divine command remains, which must surely be accomplished, and no one can resist it.

71.2.3.en: 3- This verse also speaks of the rock that accompanied the people of God in the wilderness and gave them water to drink, which is a symbol of Christ as the New Testament has declared to us (Deut 8:15).

71.3.0.en: 4- Deliver me, O my God, out of the hand of the wicked, out of the hand of the unrighteous and cruel man.

71.3.1.en: David asks God to rescue him from the wicked one, who is Satan; from the evildoer, who is everyone who obeys the thoughts of the devil and harms others; and from the unrighteous man, who is he who seizes the right of another and behaves selfishly at the expense of others. For David trusts in the hand of God, able to save him from the grasp of the wicked, because the hand of God is stronger than all men; therefore he asks with confidence, and so receives reassurance.

71.4.0.en: 5- For thou art my hope, O Lord God: thou art my trust from my youth.

71.4.1.en: All of David's petitions to God rest on two things:

71.4.2.en: a- That God is his hope, and not men or material things; therefore he asks Him for all his needs and never despairs, however much things press upon him.

71.4.3.en: b- That he has relied on God since he became aware and understood, that is, when he was a boy; so he has a long experience of relying on God, which gives him reassurance in the midst of afflictions.

71.5.0.en: 6- By thee have I been holden up from the womb: thou art he that took me out of my mother's bowels: my praise shall be continually of thee.

71.5.1.en: Here David makes clear that God is his support even while he was an unborn child, and at his coming out of the womb. For God is the One who formed him in his mother's womb, and the One who brought him out of his mother's womb as a newborn, and then consequently takes care of him throughout his life, and therefore he relies on Him. For God knows his origin, so He is able to lead him and guide him in all his steps. And for all this care he praises Him and thanks Him at all times. The verses (vv. 5, 6) in this Psalm resemble (Ps 22:9, 10) and also resemble the words of the prophet Jeremiah (Jer 1:5).

71.6.0.en: 7- I am as a wonder unto many; but thou art my strong refuge.

71.6.1.en: David endured many sufferings and passed through afflictions, but God rescued him, so he became an example and a model, and a wonder of the great work of God among men; that is, he became a light for the world to be imitated by the righteous, so that they take refuge in God, the strong refuge in every affliction, to enjoy His wonderful work in them. And David here is a symbol of Christ, who fulfilled all righteousness and bore the sufferings alone on the Cross for our salvation, and all His children walk after His likeness, as the Apostle Paul said, "we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men" (1 Cor 4:9-13). That is, as Christ was the light of the world, so He also commanded His followers to be the light of the world.

71.7.0.en: 8- Let my mouth be filled with thy praise and with thy honour all the day.

71.7.1.en: After the Psalmist tasted the work of God in afflictions, his heart clung to the love of God, and he forgot the pains of the afflictions, and his chief occupation became the glorification of God throughout his day. Thus he passed from sorrow to joy, and this is one of the most important blessings of praise.

71.7.2.en: If you meet with afflictions in your life, hasten and look to God your refuge, and ask for His help, and He will bring you through the midst of afflictions, and you will rejoice in His fellowship, and your heart will be lifted up in praising Him and thanking Him.

71.8.0.en: 9- Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth.

71.8.1.en: 1- David asks God to keep protecting him and supporting him in his old age, because old age is accompanied by weakness of the body and inability to fight enemies, and this proves that David wrote this Psalm at the end of his life, that is, in his sixties. David died at the age of seventy, and it is well known that David was a man of war from his youth, and was a military commander in the army of Saul, and then after he became king. But when he grew old, the commanders of his army asked him to rest so that he would not be exposed to the dangers of war (2 Sam 21:17).

71.8.2.en: 2- The time of old age, from the spiritual side, is a period of lukewarmness and spiritual weakness, and therefore the spiritual person asks God not to leave him in his weakness and spiritual old age, but to raise him up and encourage him.

71.9.0.en: 10- For mine enemies speak against me; and they that lay wait for my soul take counsel together,

71.9.1.en: 11- Saying, God hath forsaken him: persecute and take him; for there is none to deliver him.

71.9.2.en: 1- David's enemies seized the opportunity of his weakness because of his old age, for they were always watching him, and they said that he was weak and could be attacked, and then they falsely claimed that God had forsaken him and would not rescue him from their hands. In this they deceived themselves, and tried to make David think that he was weak and without support so that he would be afraid. But David remained firm in his faith until the end of his life; indeed, at the end of his life, when his son Adonijah tried to seize the kingdom, he issued a decree making Solomon king as his successor, and this was indeed done (1 Kgs 1:29).

71.9.3.en: 2- These two verses apply to Christ in His last sufferings and His crucifixion, especially when He cried out on the Cross, saying, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Mt 27:43). All this Satan said against Christ, and the wicked Jews repeated it after him; but Satan was surprised after the death of Christ that He seized Satan and bound him, and released the believers from Hades and brought them up to Paradise; for Satan thought that he would seize the spirit of Christ and put it in Hades, like the rest of men. So Satan always tries to fight the children of God through their weak points, whether in their old age or at any other time, to draw them away from God.

71.10.0.en: 12- O God, be not far from me: O my God, make haste for my help.

71.10.1.en: David, in the weakness of old age, with the claims and threats of his enemies, had nothing before him but to take refuge in God. So he asked Him not to be far from him, but to keep supporting him and helping him, and when the enemies see that God is near him, they fear and flee.

71.11.0.en: 13- Let them be confounded and consumed that are adversaries to my soul; let them be covered with reproach and dishonour that seek my hurt. Because of David's confidence in God, he believes that He will support him in his weakness, so that the falsehood and claims of his enemies are exposed, and indeed shame, disgrace and dishonour cover them, and they become liable to destruction, that is, God scatters them because of their evil.

71.12.0.en: 14- But I will hope continually, and will yet praise thee more and more.

71.12.1.en: 1- David's faith increased, so he had a continual hope in God that does not waver, whatever the afflictions or threats.

71.12.2.en: 2- Also, before the wonderful works of God and His protection of David, his praise and his thanks to God increased. For through praise the eyes of the one who praises are enlightened, so he sees everything new in the works of God with him, and thanks Him for them, and then God increases His mercies and support to this thankful person, so that his thanks and praise increase as well.

71.13.0.en: 15- My mouth shall shew forth thy righteousness and thy salvation all the day; for I know not the numbers thereof.

71.13.1.en: 1- When David sees the works of God in a world full of injustice, he speaks and proclaims the justice of God who rejects all injustice; and though He is long-suffering toward the unjust, and the righteous endure sufferings for a time, yet He delivers them from the hands of the wicked and saves them. And His kindnesses to them are hard to count because they are very many. This is what David experienced; for he met many afflictions from Saul and Absalom and from many others, but God rescued him from their hands and was glorified.

71.13.2.en: 2- David speaks of the justice of God all the day, that is, he praises God throughout his life, and thanks Him in affliction and in ease.

71.14.0.en: 16- I will go in the strength of the Lord God: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only.

71.14.2.en: 1- After all this praise David feels great confidence in himself, and a power by which he overcomes all his enemies. He expresses this power with "strength" (jabarut), but he ascribes this power to God; so he glorifies God and declares his humility before Him, that is, he does not steal the glory of God, and to the humble God gives power without limit.

71.14.3.en: 2- David praises none but God alone, for He alone is righteous, perfect in His righteousness, and he does not ascribe glory to himself, nor to any pagan god, nor to any power in the world, but the cause of every blessing and virtue in his life is from God, and all his good works also are from God.

71.14.4.en: The more you thank God and ascribe the glory to Him, the more your heart rejoices in God, and God rejoices in you, and your life delights in fellowship with God, and many mercies overflow upon you; indeed your eyes are enlightened and God reveals to you His secrets which surpass the mind.

71.14.5.en: 3- Thanksgiving and proclamation of the great things of God (vv. 17-24):

71.15.0.en: 17- O God, thou hast taught me from my youth: and hitherto have I declared thy wondrous works.

71.15.1.en: David declares God's care for him, for He taught him how to walk in his way from his youth, so he enjoyed fellowship with God from the beginning of his life, and learned how to pray and praise God, and once he tasted the sweetness of praise he was no longer able to leave it, so prayer and praise became his life, until he said, "But I give myself unto prayer" (Ps 109:4).

71.16.0.en: 18- Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come.

71.16.1.en: David repeats his request for God's presence with him in the time of old age and grey hair, not only to help him in the weakness of old age, as mentioned in (v. 9), but also that he may remain strong in his faith and his love for God, so that he can serve and preach to those around him, that is, tell them about the mighty God, who is able to support His children with His strong arm, and teach every child and youth who has come into the world how to live with God. In this David shows his concern for being discipled at the hand of God to the end of his life, and also his concern for discipling all those around him so that they may know God.

71.17.0.en: 19- Thy righteousness also, O God, is very high, who hast done great things: O God, who is like unto thee!

71.17.1.en: 1- David describes the righteousness of God as being high and exceedingly lofty; it is above all the gods, because they are demons, which the pagans think to be gods; He does great things with His children, and there is none like Him. For if the first Adam fell when he wanted to become, like God, a knower of good and evil, David, who is a symbol of Christ, the second Adam, declares that there is none like God.

71.17.2.en: 2- The righteousness of God is His love and His faithfulness in caring for His children, from Adam until today, and it is also His Incarnation and His giving of Himself for the redemption of mankind.

71.18.0.en: 20- Thou, which hast shewed me great and sore troubles, shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth.

71.18.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm here prophesies about the children of Israel in the land of Egypt, who endured bitter slavery and many labors, but God gave them life anew by their crossing of the Red Sea and their going up to the wilderness of Sinai, and their deliverance from Pharaoh and his army who were drowned.

71.18.2.en: 2- This verse is also a prophecy about the captivity that the people of Israel suffered, but God revived them anew by bringing them back from the captivity and taking them up to Jerusalem to build the Temple.

71.18.3.en: 3- This verse likewise prophesies about Christ in His sufferings and crucifixion, but He returned to life by His Resurrection and ascended into the heavens. It also applies to every person who repents and suffers the pains of leaving sin, and then returns to life, and so ascends and rises above every sin and evil desire.

71.19.0.en: 21- Thou shalt increase my greatness, and comfort me on every side.

71.19.1.en: 1- David affirms the work of God with His children, whose example is David himself, for God gives him many blessings, so he becomes very great and his heart is comforted by the work of His Holy Spirit in him, to compensate him for all that he endured of afflictions. Thus after David endured the pursuits of Saul, then Absalom, God returned and magnified him, and he triumphed over all his enemies around him.

71.19.2.en: 2- This also is what happens with every believer in Christ, for after he was condemned to death he enjoys the redemption of Christ, and regains his greatness as a man, and the Holy Spirit dwells in him to comfort him all his days.

71.20.0.en: 22- I will also praise thee with the psaltery, even thy truth, O my God: unto thee will I sing with the harp, O thou Holy One of Israel.

71.20.1.en: 23- My lips shall greatly rejoice when I sing unto thee; and my soul, which thou hast redeemed. 24- My tongue also shall talk of thy righteousness all the day long: for they are confounded, for they are brought unto shame, that seek my hurt.

71.20.2.en: 1- David ends the Psalm with the praise of God, using musical instruments such as the psaltery and the harp. This is what God deserves from the man whom He created, for all His righteousness and holiness, indeed His gifts and His support of His children and their deliverance from their enemies, so that the enemies receive shame and disgrace. And the children of God lift up not only their tongues and their lips, but their souls as well, in praise and thanksgiving to God.

71.20.3.en: 2- If thanksgiving to God was a duty in the Old Testament for all His great works with His children, how much more does He deserve thanks and glorification in the New Testament, for His redemption, which saved them from Satan and gave them life with Him, and then the Kingdom of Heaven.

71.20.4.en: How great is the praise of God! It is not only a duty toward Him, but it also gladdens our hearts, so that we live in constant joy and attachment to eternal life.

71.20.5.en: The Kingdom of God, for Solomon: "Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son" (v. 1). Introduction:

71.20.6.en: 1- Its writer: a- King Solomon, and he may have had in mind the instructions of his father David to him when he made him king.

71.20.7.en: b- There is another opinion that its writer is the prophet David, and that he addressed it to Solomon his son when he made him king, that he might be a true king as God wants.

71.20.8.en: 2- This Psalm tells us about the kingdom of God, its characteristics and its blessings, and it is an example and model for all states and kingdoms in the world throughout the generations.

71.20.9.en: 3- This Psalm speaks clearly about Christ, for it is a Messianic Psalm, and because Solomon is a symbol of Christ, there are verses that cannot apply except to Christ (vv. 8, 11, 17).

71.20.10.en: 4- This Psalm is liturgical, and it was recited in the Church anciently on the feasts of the Nativity and the Baptism.

71.20.11.en: 5- With the end of this Psalm the second book of the Psalms ends, as the Jews divided it, which includes (Ps 42-72). Therefore the reader notices that the last verses of this Psalm end with the word Amen, then Amen, Alleluia. Then after the end of this Psalm it adds and says, "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended", because the writer of most of the Psalms in this part is the prophet David, like the rest of the five books of the Psalms. It does not mean that David did not write the following books, but it only means the end of the second book.

71.20.12.en: 6- There is a resemblance between this Psalm and the last part of the Book of Exodus (Ex 25-40), where it tells us of God's kingship over His people through the Tabernacle of Meeting.

71.20.13.en: There is also a resemblance between this Psalm and the Book of Isaiah (Isa 11:1-5; 60-62).

71.20.14.en: 7- This Psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
